title: How to Slice Brussels Sprouts Thin for Shaved Salads
meta_description: Master the art of thinly sliced Brussels sprouts for salads with a mandoline. Learn step‑by‑step tips, safety tricks, and how a mandoline slicer makes shaved Br
html:
Thin, delicate shreds of Brussels sprouts add crunch, peppery flavor, and a pop of green to any salad. The secret to getting those restaurant‑thin ribbons? A good mandoline slicer. In this guide we’ll walk through preparation, blade selection, safe technique, and finishing touches so you can turn a bag of Brussels sprouts into a salad‑star in minutes.

Why a Mandoline Is the Best Tool for Shaved Brussels Sprouts

When you reach for a razor‑sharp knife, you’ll find the sprouts tend to tear or produce uneven pieces. A mandoline slicer gives you consistent, restaurant‑thin, even slices with minimal effort. The Mandoline Slicer offers adjustable thickness settings and a built‑in hand guard, which means you can dial in the exact blade height for shaved Brussels sprouts mandoline style and stay safe while you work.

Preparing the Sprouts for the Mandoline

Start with fresh sprouts that are firm and bright green. Follow these quick prep steps:

  1. Trim the ends. Cut off the woody stem tip—about a quarter‑inch is enough.
  2. Remove the outer leaves. Peel away any yellowed or wilted leaves; they can interfere with the blade.
  3. Halve or quarter. For the mandoline to work smoothly, slice the sprout in half lengthwise. If your mandoline’s opening is narrow, quarter the halves.
  4. Dry the pieces. Pat them with a towel. Moisture makes the blade stick and can cause uneven cuts.

These steps keep the sprouts stable on the platform and help the blade glide cleanly.

Setting Up Your Mandoline for Shaved Brussels Sprouts

Adjust the thickness dial to the thinnest setting—usually labeled “0” or “paper thin.” If you prefer a slightly sturdier bite, move the knob up one notch; you’ll still get a fine ribbon, just a tad more texture. Attach the hand guard and make sure the blade is securely locked. The Mandoline Slicer has a clear safety lock that prevents the blade from moving while you’re not slicing.

Safety First: Using the Hand Guard Effectively

The hand guard isn’t just a convenience; it’s essential when you’re slicing something as small as Brussels sprouts. Here’s a quick safety checklist:

  • Hold the guard firmly with your fingertips curled around the handle—never place fingers near the blade.
  • Slide the sprouts against the guard, not the blade itself.
  • Never try to force a sprout that’s too large; cut it down to size first.
  • When you’re done, disengage the blade lock before cleaning.

Following these steps eliminates the most common mandoline accidents and keeps your hands intact for the next round of slicing.

Getting Perfectly Shaved Sprouts

With the mandoline set, place a half‑sprout on the platform, guard side down, and press gently against the blade. Use a smooth, steady motion—let the mandoline do the work. You’ll see a cascade of thin ribbons fall onto your cutting board. If the sprouts start to bunch, pause, shake the board, and resume. This prevents the blade from catching and ensures uniform thickness.

Once you’ve sliced the entire batch, give the shreds a quick toss with a pinch of salt. The salt draws out a little moisture, which softens the raw bite and helps the sprouts absorb dressing later.

Finishing Your Shaved Brussels Sprout Salad

Now that you have a bowl of delicate sprouts, it’s time to assemble the salad. Here are a few tried‑and‑true combos:

  • Classic vinaigrette. Whisk together olive oil, lemon juice, Dijon mustard, honey, and a dash of pepper. Toss with the shreds, toasted almonds, and shaved Parmesan.
  • Asian‑inspired. Mix soy sauce, rice vinegar, sesame oil, and a pinch of ginger. Add toasted sesame seeds, sliced radishes, and a handful of cilantro.
  • Fruit‑sweet. Combine orange segments, pomegranate arils, and a drizzle of maple‑balsamic glaze for a bright, sweet‑savory contrast.

Because the sprouts are so thin, they absorb dressing quickly, so add the vinaigrette just before serving to keep the salad crisp.

Cleaning and Maintaining Your Mandoline

After you’ve enjoyed your salad, clean the mandoline while the blade is still warm (but not hot). Rinse the platform and guard under running water, using a brush to dislodge any vegetable fibers. Never submerge the entire unit if it has wooden handles—wipe them dry immediately. Store the slicer with the blade covered or in a protective case to keep it sharp for your next kitchen adventure.

FAQ

Can I use a mandoline for other leafy vegetables?

Absolutely. Kale, cabbage, and even bok choy slice beautifully on a mandoline. Just adjust the thickness setting and use the hand guard for safety.

Do I need a special blade for Brussels sprouts?

No special blade is required. The standard straight blade on the Mandoline Slicer works perfectly for shaved Brussels sprouts. If you want crisper, wavy ribbons, many mandolines offer a julienne attachment that can be swapped in.

Is it okay to slice frozen Brussels sprouts?

It’s best to thaw them first. Frozen sprouts are too hard for the blade and can cause chipping or uneven cuts. Once thawed and patted dry, treat them the same as fresh sprouts.
